editorial_contributions.text: An integer distance graph is a graph \(G(D)\) with the set of integers as the vertex set and with an edge joining two vertices \(a\) and \(b\) iff \(|a-b|\in D\), where \(D\) is a subset of the positive integers. The authors determine the chromatic numbers of integer distance graphs (i) if \(D\) consists of two different positive integers together with their sum and their (positive) differences and (ii) with finite or infinite distance sets which are arithmetical sequences.

title.title: Improved upper bounds for six-valent integer distance graph coloring periods

editorial_contributions.text: An integer distance graph is a graph \(G(D)\) with the set of integers as vertex set and two vertices \(u\) and \(v\) adjacent if and only if \(|u-v|\in D\). The so-called distance set \(D\) is a subset of the positive integers. In this paper the chromatic number \(\chi (G(D))\) and the choice number \(\text{ch}(G(D))\) of \(G(D)\) are determined in case that \(D=\{x,2x,\ldots ,nx,y\}\), \(\text{gcd}(x,y)\)=1. It is known that \(\chi (G(D))\leq \text{ch}(G(D))\leq |D|+1\) and conjectured by Zhu that \(\chi (G(D))=|D|+1\) implies \(\omega (G(D))\geq |D|\). It is shown that \(\omega (G(D))\geq |D|\) if and only if \(|D|\leq 1\) or \(D=\{x,y,x+y\}\) or \(D=\{x,y,x+y,|y-x|\}\) or \(D=\{x,2x,\ldots ,nx,y\}\) with \(x\neq y\).

editorial_contributions.text: An integer distance graph is a graph \(G(D)\) with the set of integers as vertex set and with an edge joining two vertices \(u\) and \(v\) if and only if \(|u-v|\in D\) where \(D\) is a subset of the set of positive integers. If \(D\) is a subset of the set \(P\) of primes then \(G(D)\) is called prime distance graph. Since \(\chi (G(D))=4\) if \(D=\{2,3,5\}\) or \(D=P\) where \(\chi (G(D))\) is the chromatic number of \(G(D)\) \textit{R. B. Eggleton} et al. [Discrete Math. 69, 105 (1988)] posed the problem to characterize all sets \(D\) of primes with: If \(|D|=4\), then, if and only if \(\{2,3,5\} \subset D\), \(D=\{2,3,p,p+2\}\) or \(D\) is one of eight particular cases. Therefore, \textit{A. Kemnitz} and \textit{H. Kolberg} [Discrete Math. 191, 113-123 (1998; Zbl 0956.05044)] raised the question: Is there, for every fixed cardinal, only a finite collection of minimum sets \(D \subset P\) of the given size (i.e. no proper subset of \(D\) has chromatic number 4) for which \(D\) is without twin primes and \(\chi (G(D))=4\)? The main result of this note is: If Schinzel's conjecture on irreducible polynomials is true then there exist infinitely many such \(D\) of cardinality 5.

title.title: On a question concerning prime distance graphs

editorial_contributions.text: If \(D\) is a subset of the positive integers, then the integer distance graph \(G(\mathbb Z,D)\) is defined as the graph with vertex set \(V(G(\mathbb Z,D))=\mathbb Z\), the set of integers, and two vertices \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent if and only if their distance \(| u-v|\) is an element of the so-called distance set \(D\). In this paper the chromatic number \(\chi(G(\mathbb Z,D))\) is determined for some 4-element distance sets \(D\) containing \(\{2,3\}\) as a subset and for some 5-element distance sets \(D\) containing \(\{2,3,5\}\) as a subset.

title.title: Coloring of some integer distance graphs

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: A connected Cayley graph on an abelian group with a finite generating set $S$ can be represented by its Heuberger matrix, i.e., an integer matrix whose columns generate the group of relations between members of $S$. In a previous article, the authors laid the foundation for the use of Heuberger matrices to study chromatic numbers of abelian Cayley graphs. We call the number of rows in the Heuberger matrix the {\it dimension}, and the number of columns the {\it rank}. In this paper, we give precise numerical conditions that completely determine the chromatic number in all cases with dimension $1$; with rank $1$; and with dimension $\leq 3$ and rank $\leq 2$. For such a graph without loops, we show that it is $4$-colorable if and only if it does not contain a $5$-clique, and it is $3$-colorable if and only if it contains neither a diamond lanyard nor a $C_{13}(1,5)$, both of which we define herein. It is shown in another paper that as a special case of our theorem for dimension $3$ and rank $2$, we obtain improved upper bounds for minimal periods of optimal colorings of $6$-valent integer distance graphs.

title.title: Chromatic numbers of Cayley graphs of abelian groups: Cases of small dimension and rank

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Jacobson, Levin, and Scheinerman introduced the fractional Ramsey function \(r_{f} (a_{1}, a_{2},\dots , a_k)\) as an extension of the classical definition for Ramsey numbers. They determined an exact formula for the fractional Ramsey function for the case \(k=2\). In this article, we answer an open problem by determining an explicit formula for the general case \(k>2\) by constructing an infinite family of circulant graphs for which the independence numbers can be computed explicitly. This construction gives us two further results: a new (infinite) family of star extremal graphs which are a superset of many of the families currently known in the literature, and a broad generalization of known results on the chromatic number of integer distance graphs.

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper discusses the chromatic coloring of distance graphs (DG)s, especially prime distance graphs (PDG)s. A graph \(G(Z, D)\) with vertex set \(Z\) is called an integer distance graph (IDG) if its edge set is obtained by joining two elements of \(Z\) by an edge whenever their absolute difference is a member of \(D\). If \(D = P\) or \(D \subseteq P\), where \(P\) is the set of all prime numbers (i.e., \(G(Z, P)\)), then it is called a prime distance graph (PDG). Since coloring a PDG is equivalent to producing a prime distance labeling (PDL) for vertices of \(G\), this paper gives PDL for certain classes of all graphs too. The paper blends graph coloring with number theory.

The paper is divided into seven sections. The first section is the introduction, where the basic notions are described. The second section is about the coloring of IDGs. Then, the coloring of various PDGs is proved in the third section. Some important results, which are prerequisites to prove distance graphs, especially PDGs are explained in the fourth section. While the fifth section is about some existence results on PDGs, the sixth section gives some general results. The final section is the conclusion.

The introduction explains various terminologies used in the article. Suppose that \((Y, \sigma)\) is a metric space. Let \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in Y\). Then, \(\sigma(\alpha_1, \alpha_2)\) implies the separation distance (SD). Let \(D = \{i : 0 <i< \infty\}\). If \(V (G) = Y\) and \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in Y\) is deemed to be adjacent if and only if \(\sigma(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) \in D\), then \(G(Y,D)\) is called a DG. The chromatic number of \(G\) is denoted as \( \chi (G(Y,D))\). Moreover, if \(D = \{\alpha \}\) with \(\alpha> 0\), then the corresponding graph is a DG with \(\sigma\) as Euclidean distance metric. Even though finding \(\chi (G(\mathbb{R}, \{1\}))\) is simple, finding \(\chi(G(\mathbb{R}^2, \{1\}))\) becomes extremely hard and got included as one of the most selected problems of all time by Paul Erdős. If \(f: V (G) \to \mathbb{R}^2\) is an embedding with the attribute that \(|f(\alpha)- f(\beta)| = 1\) whenever \((\alpha, \beta) \in E(G)\), the edge set of \(G\), then \(G(V,E)\) is called a unit distance graph (UDG). Let \(D = \{i : 0 <i< \infty \}\) and \(r \in \mathbb{Q}^+\), then for any \(k \in \mathbb{Z}^+\), \(\chi(G(\mathbb{Q}^k, D)) = \chi(G(\mathbb{Q}^k, rD))\).

The second section concentrates on coloring of IDGs \(G(Z, D)\) with \(D \subseteq P\). Let \(G(\mathbb{Z}^+,D)\) be an IDG with \(D \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^+\). It is understood that \( \alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in \mathbb{Z}^+\) with \( \alpha_1< \alpha_2\) are linked by drawing an edge if and only if \( \alpha_2 - \alpha_1 \in D\). But it is difficult to identify those \(D\) with \(\chi(G(\mathbb{Z}, D)) < \infty\). With the help of the Katznelson-Razza conjecture, which says that \(\chi(G(\mathbb{Z}, D)) < \infty \iff D\) can be written as the union of a finite number of lonely sets, one can try for a solution.

The third section is about the coloring of PDGs. \textit{R. B. Eggleton} et al. coined the term PDG in [J. Comb. Theory, Ser. B 39, 86--100 (1985; Zbl 0549.05029)]. One can deem \(G(Z, P)\) as a PDG if one can produce a \(1-1\) labeling \(g: V (G) \to Z\) with the property that any member of \(E(G)\), say \((\alpha, \beta)\), possesses a prime distance between them. That is, \(|g(\alpha)- g(\beta)| = g((\alpha, \beta)) \in P\). In a PDL, the labels allotted to the elements of \(V(G)\) must be non-repeating. However, the labels that result from this labeling on the elements of \(E(G)\) need not be nonrepeating. Further, in a DG, \(G(Z, D)\) a non-edge may possess a prime distance. This, however, will not happen for PDG, and \(G(Z, P)\), as every prime number distance warrants an edge between them.

The section ``Some motivational results from number theory'' gives some pertinent properties of integers that have acted as sources of inspiration to obtain the PDL of certain classes of graphs.

The fifth section ``Some existence results on PDGs'' is a lengthy section with six theorems. Results concerning the existence of PDGs belonging to classes 2, 3, or 4 whose distance sets are subsets of \(P\) with varied cardinality are proved here. The theorems are proved with the help of the Green-Tao theorem, the Goldbach conjecture, the twin prime conjecture, and mathematical induction. Theorem 5 and Theorem 6 have lengthy proofs. The theorems are:
\begin{itemize}
\item[1.] Suppose that \(D = \{p-(c-1)s, p-(c-2)s,\ldots, p-s, p, p + s, p + 2s,\ldots, p + (d-2)s, p + (d-1)s\}\). Then, there exists a PDG \(G(Z, D)\) in class 2.
\item[2.] Suppose that \(D = \{2, p_1\}\) where \(p_1\) is that prime with \(p_1 + p_2 = 2s-4\) where \(s\ge 6\) and \(p_2 \in P\). Then there exists a PDG \(G(Z, D)\) in class 2 or class 3, depending on whether \(s \in 2 Z\) or \(s \in 2 Z + 1\).
\item[3.] Suppose that \(D = \{2, p_1, p_2\}\), where \(p_1, p_2 \in P\) are twin primes. Then there exists a PDG \(G(Z, D)\) in class 3.
\item[4.] Suppose that \(D = \{2, 5, 7\}\). Then, there exists a prime-distance square graph \(G(Z, D)\) in class 3.
\item[5.] Let \(D = \{2, 3, 5, 4^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}, 6^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}, 8^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}, (4 + \sum\limits_{j=1}^{s-1} 3 \times 2^j)^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}, \dots, (2 + \sum\limits_{j=1}^{s} 3 \times 2^j)^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}\}\), where \(s \in \mathbb N\). Then, there exists a PDG \(G\) in class 3 with \(D\) as its distance set.
\item[6.] Let D = \(\{2, 3, 5, 7, 7^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}, 10^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}, 13^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}, 16^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}, (7 + \sum\limits_{j=1}^{s-1} 4 \times 3^j)^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime}, \dots, (4 + \sum\limits_{j=1}^{s} 4 \times 3^j)^{\mathrm{th}}\text{ prime} \}\), where \(s \in \mathbb N\). Then, there exists a PDG \(G\) in class 4 with \(D\) as its distance set.
\end{itemize}

The sixth section ``Some general results'' consists of eight theorems, two corollaries, two observations, and a lemma. Note that any subgraph of a PDG is a PDG, but if any subgraph of a graph admits no PDL then the graph itself admits no PDL. The theorems in this section are:
\begin{itemize}
\item[1.] For any two graphs \(G\) and \(H\), \(\chi(G \times H) = \max\{\chi(G), \chi(H)\}\). Here, \(\times\) stands for the Cartesian product.
\item[2.] Let \(G\) be any PDG in class \(i\) for \(1 \le i \le 4\). Then \(G \times K_2\) is also a PDG of the respective class.
\item[3.] Let \(G\) be any PDG. Then, any countable union of disjoint copies of \(G\) is a PDG. Moreover, both \(G\) and \(nG\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\) belong to the same class \(i\), for \(1 \le i \le 4\).
\item[4.] The middle graph of a path on \(n\) vertices is a PDG, and it belongs to class 3.
\item[5.] The total graph of a path on \(n\) vertices is a PDG, and it belongs to class 3.
\item[6.] Let \(G\) and \(H\) be any two PDGs belonging to class \(i\) for \(3 \le i \le 4\). Then \(G \lor H\) is not a PDG.
\item[7.] \(K_5-e\) is not a PDG.
\end{itemize}

Theorem 5 and Theorem 6 of Section 5 attempt to characterise the family of graphs belonging to class \(i\) when \(D\) is of any given size and obtain one family each of graphs in classes 3 and 4 whose distance set consists of countably many elements. The last theorem of Section 6 gives a fourth proof, which is independent of any of the previously used proof techniques by other authors for ``All cycles are PDGs''.

The main methods of proof are mathematical induction and deduction. There is a good use of the results of number theory and conjectures in number theory to prove graph theoretical problems. Furthermore, functions are defined to label vertices and prove results. A lot of prime numbers are identified in order to label the edges. Some of the theorems are proved by assuming certain conjectures are true. Thus, the validity of those theorems depends heavily on the truthfulness of certain conjectures.

For Part II of this paper see [the second author et al., J. Tianjin Univ. 54, No. 10, 56--67 (2021; \url{doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FHT})].

series.title: Proyecciones

title.title: Chromatic coloring of distance graphs. III

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We extend the one-dimensional lonely set method to two dimensions for the purpose of studying the chromatic number of integer distance graphs in two dimensions. Given a lacunary sequence of displacement vectors in $Z^{2}$, we use a lacunary matrix theorem given by Broderick, Fishman and Kleinbock, to prove the existence of a satisfactory multiplier vector. We then give an explicit geometric colouring argument. This proves that any integer distance graph generated by a lacunary sequence of vectors in two dimensions has finite chromatic number.

title.title: Proof of the Finiteness of the Chromatic Number of Two-Dimensional Lacunary Distance Graphs
